scoreNote: Strong (5): rejects the criterion with strong reasons — much great art is difficult, and merit differs from popularity — then concedes that art must communicate something; well organized and persuasive.

sentences.text: Some of the most celebrated works in human history baffled their first audiences and many audiences since.
Yet the statement insists that for any work of art to have merit, it must be understandable to most people.

I disagree, because the value of art is not measured by how many people grasp it at first encounter, and a standard of mass understandability would condemn much of humanity's greatest work as worthless.

sections.role: Body — Much great art is difficult

sentences.text: First, a great deal of art widely regarded as profound is not readily understandable to most people.
Joyce's Ulysses, Picasso's late paintings, and much of classical poetry demand an effort, background, and patience that most readers and viewers simply do not bring to them.
If understandability to the majority were the test of merit, these works would fail it, and we would have to call them worthless, which is plainly absurd.
Difficulty is often the price of depth, since art that explores complex experience cannot always be flattened into something instantly clear.
A symphony's structure, a poem's allusions, a film's symbolism may reveal themselves only on the second or the tenth encounter, not the first.
The fault, in such cases, may lie with the hurried audience rather than with the demanding work.
Moreover, the statement confuses being understood with being good, which are quite separate things.
Much that is instantly understandable is shallow, and much that is difficult is deep, so accessibility tells us about an audience, not about quality.
A catchy jingle is understood by everyone and forgotten by morning, while a difficult novel that few finish can change the lives of those who do.
The worth of art lies in what it reveals, how it moves us, and how long it lasts, none of which is settled by a head count of who got it.
History is full of works ignored or scorned in their day that later generations recognized as masterpieces, which proves that majority understanding is no reliable guide to merit.
To equate merit with mass comprehension is to let the size of an audience decide the value of a work.

sections.role: Body — But art must communicate something

sentences.text: There is, however, a reasonable instinct buried in the statement.
Art does communicate, and a work understood by no one at all, that locks its meaning away entirely, may indeed fail as art.
But understandable to most people sets the bar far too low, demanding instant mass appeal rather than the possibility of understanding by a willing audience.
The right standard is not that everyone must understand a work easily, but that it must offer something real to those who meet it with attention.
Between the gibberish that communicates nothing and the jingle that communicates only the obvious lies the vast territory of serious art.

vocab.gloss: 胡言亂語；難以理解的東西

sentences.text: In conclusion, art need not be understandable to most people in order to have merit.
Difficulty is often the companion of depth, and the value of a work is decided by what it offers those who engage with it, not by how large a crowd grasps it instantly.
The measure of art is not how many understand it, but how much there is to understand.
